03 / Selected work

Seven pieces from the PGP. Six arguments and one thing that runs.

A teen-skincare category play for a real dermatology brand that reached the national round of its competition; four ventures argued from scratch; one sector taken apart; and a booking automation built rather than diagrammed. All of it is team work, credited as such, and every case below says what the argument was and where it could break.

Project 01 · Case competition entry · Team Remedy Rebels

#OwnYourSpot

A teen-first repositioning for Benzac Power Patch, written for Galderma's GRAD 3.0 challenge — turn acne care from something you hide into something you own. Selected for the national round.

Don’t make teenagers choose between effective and expressive.

From the deck · Target & Opportunity

The brief

Galderma's GRAD challenge asked for a route to a ₹100 Cr brand in India. The team took the harder reading of it — not "how do we sell more patches," but who forms the acne-care habit, and when.

What the research turned up

The team ran a primary survey of teenagers aged 13–18, analysed 100+ responses, and interviewed dermatologists and school counsellors to sanity-check what they were hearing. The finding that reframed the brief: 94.3% said acne sometimes or almost always affects their confidence or makes them hesitate to speak up. Nearly half either do nothing about it or squeeze the spot. Three in four already know pimple patches — barely one in ten have used Benzac's.

So the format wasn't the unknown. The brand was.

The idea

Teenagers were being made to choose between clinical — trusted, effective, faintly medical — and trend-led, which is fun but carries no dermatological authority. #OwnYourSpot refuses the choice. Treat, express, trust: a clinically backed 3-in-1 patch (hydrocolloid, salicylic acid, Centella asiatica) in five wearable designs — moon, cloud, star, thunder, wings — so treatment becomes self-expression rather than concealment.

It runs out through five hero initiatives: dermatologist-led sessions in schools, teen creators telling real acne stories, an #OwnYourSpot community, clinical credibility from practising dermatologists, and omnichannel availability.

Where it lands

A four-phase, 24-month rollout — prove, scale urban, expand, nationalise — with an explicit gate at each boundary. Scale only if the pilot's rate-of-sale hurdle is met. Fix the low-velocity cluster before adding doors. Reconcile actuals against the ₹100 Cr bridge before resetting Year 3.

The call worth defending

The deck refuses to present ₹100 Cr as a forecast. It calls it "a hypothesis worth stress-testing out loud," then does the arithmetic against the category it would have to come from — roughly ₹252 Cr today — and states the uncomfortable consequence plainly: ₹100 Cr means about 40% of current category value, from one brand. Distribution alone cannot get there. Most competition decks would have buried that. This one put it on the page and then built the plan around it.

Project 02 · Course project · D2C brand build

Giggle

Premium spill-resistant playwear, and the argument that a seven-year customer is a pricing architecture rather than a catalogue.

Because childhood is not meant to be clean. It’s meant to be lived.

From the deck · Our Story

The problem

The team named it the modern parenting paradox: parents want to protect the clothes, children need to explore the world, and today you have to pick one. Constant laundry, daycare stain anxiety, ruined premium outfits, the stress of three changes a day — against the fact that messy play is how young children develop.

The gap they found

India's children's apparel market runs to USD 22.6B, kidswear to USD 11.1B. Premium functional playwear is under 1% of it. Mapped on style against fabric technology, the quadrant is empty: FirstCry sits basic and fast-fashion, SuperBottoms and Kidbea sit functional but not premium, boutiques sit premium but on plain cotton. Nobody occupies both axes.

What the team built

A dual-layer garment as the product answer — a cotton-polyester outer with a PFAS-free stain-resistant finish, over a 100% organic cotton and bamboo viscose inner for sensitive skin. Then three moats: supply-chain lock-ins on the material science, a brand sitting where aesthetics meets utility, and proprietary sizing and wear data coming back from D2C customers.

The model

Unit economics at a ₹1,900 average order: 60% gross margin, ₹350–400 acquisition cost, ₹600–650 contribution per order. Year-three targets of a ₹100 Cr run rate, 40%+ repeat purchase and ₹18,000+ lifetime value per customer.

The call worth defending

Pricing is tiered by the child's age, not by season — ₹499 for a tee at ages 1–3, ₹699 at 3–5, ₹899 at 6–8. It reads like a small merchandising decision and it isn't. It converts the one thing about this customer nobody can change — that the child keeps growing — into a revenue curve. Acquire at age one and you have bought seven years of rising basket size, which is what actually makes the acquisition cost defensible.

Project 03 · Course project · Decoding Business Models

The Sichuan Project

India's first build-your-own Sichuan mala bowl bar, argued from a single insight about taste rather than trend.

Mala doesn’t ask Indians to acquire a new taste.

From the deck · The Insight

The insight the whole deck rests on

The rest of that line matters as much as the first half: it offers a taste we already love, in a format that doesn't exist here yet. Delhi NCR eats spice for breakfast and has been eating Indo-Chinese for decades. What's missing isn't the flavour — it's the everyday price point and the self-serve format.

The gap

Mala in India is stuck in premium mode: ₹1,200-plus, sit-down or delivery, an event rather than a habit. Meanwhile two million-plus office workers around Cyber Hub are cycling between tiffin, thali and Subway. The weigh-and-pay bowl bar is proven in Singapore, Bangkok, Frankfurt and Chengdu, and has no direct competitor in India.

The concept

Pick, weigh, choose, cook. Twenty-five-plus ingredients at ₹90 per 100g, dry Xiang Guo or soupy Mala Tang, spice level to taste, fired in under five minutes. Average bowl 400g, average ticket ₹380, door to bowl in fifteen minutes. The customer watches the scale and the bill — no fixed menu, no hidden pricing.

The economics

₹30L to open. ₹4L a month to run. At ninety bowls a day, ₹11.4L monthly revenue against ₹4L of cost. The ask is ₹15L for a first site near Cyber Hub, built as a template to replicate.

The call worth defending

Two things this deck does that most F&B pitches won't. First, it publishes two break-even numbers — a 4–6 month base case and a 6–9 month realistic case — instead of quietly presenting the flattering one. Second, it deliberately withholds Zomato and Swiggy until month two, after dine-in habits have formed, treating delivery as a top-up channel rather than the crutch that quietly eats the margin.

Project 04 · Course project · Marketplace design

One Shoot, Every Bharat

A vernacular-first creator marketplace — one shoot becomes an ad that speaks every region's language.

One creator shoot → one ad that speaks every region’s language.

From the deck · Cover

The problem, stated twice

Matching is broken on both sides. Brands burn time screening hundreds of applicants for aesthetic fit and reliability, or fall back on agencies that don't scale. Creators apply broadly to campaigns they were never going to win and get no feedback on why. Neither side accumulates a trust signal — every campaign starts from zero.

The wedge

Around 85% of Indian OTT viewership is regional-language, and localised video drives roughly 22% higher return than English-first campaigns. Yet every incumbent — JoinBrands, Billo, Aspire, Insense — is built English-first, one creator per market. A brand that wants five regions books five shoots.

What the team designed

A marketplace with a matching engine that ranks creators against a brief and learns from completed-campaign outcomes, plus the piece that makes it a different business: an AI language-multiplication layer. One authentic shoot is dubbed and lip-synced into Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Marathi — orchestrated through existing APIs rather than built from scratch.

The model

About 15% commission on self-serve; a retainer with a lower per-transaction rate for managed enterprise accounts; featured placement and analytics as later upsells. Pricing is per campaign package — creator videos plus language variants, tiered by number of regional markets — rather than per creator, which is how everyone else prices.

The call worth defending

An authenticity and dub-fidelity score, built into the product as a gate rather than bolted on as a feature. Dubbing at volume is the easy part; the failure mode is dubbed content that stops feeling like UGC and starts feeling like an over-produced ad, at which point the entire value proposition collapses. Making that a scored, blocking quality gate is the team betting the product on the thing most likely to kill it.

Project 05 · Course project · Seed pitch format · Team 10

ClauseIQ

AI contract review for the legal teams that can't afford enterprise contract review.

From four hours of redlines to twenty minutes of certainty.

From the deck · Cover

The problem

Contract review is a bottleneck every growing business hits, and only enterprises can afford to fix it. Roughly 60% of a lawyer's time goes on reviewing contracts rather than advising the business; a mid-size commercial contract takes about four hours by hand; enterprise review platforms start around $50K a year. Small legal teams either eat the risk of skipping proper review or eat the cost of counsel the business can't justify.

The product

Three steps. Upload and parse — every clause extracted and mapped against the team's own playbook and past agreements. AI analysis — non-standard, risky or missing clauses flagged, each with a risk score and a plain-English explanation of the exposure. Review and export — accept redlines in one click, out to a tracked-changes Word file or an e-sign tool.

The model

Tiered subscriptions priced against the cost of the problem rather than against enterprise tools: $79, $249 and $599 a month, plus usage overage, annual billing discount and white-label API licensing for legal-tech and fintech platforms. The ask is $750K to reach 200 paying teams and $500K ARR inside twelve months.

The call worth defending

The lead magnet is a free, no-signup tool that scans a single clause. It looks like a growth tactic and it's really a positioning decision: the one objection a sceptical legal buyer cannot be talked out of is accuracy, so the go-to-market gives away the proof rather than arguing for it — and captures intent-rich leads at exactly the moment the buyer is convinced.

Project 06 · Sector analysis · Group 5

The Indian Service Marketplace

India's home-services market taken apart layer by layer — three waves, five layers, and one incumbent caught between them.

Can convenience become a habit without destroying marketplace economics?

From the deck · Closing question

The subject

India's home-services market is overwhelmingly informal — no standardisation, no accountability, no scale. The team traced how platforms impose order on it, and what that costs.

The structure they imposed

Three waves: informal word-of-mouth, then digital marketplaces with verified professionals and ratings, then instant — 10 to 60 minute fulfilment. The industry moving from "find someone" to "get it done now" is not a marketing shift; it's a different platform architecture. Underneath that, a five-layer sector map — demand, service, supply, platform, and the infrastructure and regulation layer that most analyses leave out.

The case at the centre

Urban Company's dilemma, stated as a tension rather than a verdict: a profitable, growing core marketplace funding InstaHelp's loss-making push into instant services, with revenue up 36% year on year. Around it, Snabbit betting on hyper-local supply density across five cities and Pronto differentiating on guaranteed shift-based worker income across four.

The finding on tier-2 and tier-3

The metro playbook doesn't scale. Density is the constraint, not demand. What works instead is category-led entry — one high-frequency service customers already understand — then clustering to make each technician productive before opening the next area, with supply trained and retained locally rather than flown in.

The call worth defending

The analysis includes a slide on what isn't known. It lists the worker-side issues reported by labour organisations and media — opaque rating, allocation and penalty systems, income volatility, weak grievance mechanisms — and then states plainly that there is no publicly disclosed, independently audited data on suspension rates and appeal outcomes, partner attrition, penalty incidence or social-security coverage. Naming the research gap instead of filling it with an estimate is the harder, better choice, and it turns a governance footnote into a stated material risk.

Project 07 · Course exercise · Automation, built in Make

Urban Services Booking Workflow

The operational counterpart to the sector analysis — the booking flow those decks describe, built rather than diagrammed.

What it does

A webhook takes an inbound booking — customer name, service type, location, email. A router splits the flow on service type: cleaning down one branch, everything else down the other. Each branch writes the booking into a shared data store with a timestamp, then sends a notification email that names the customer, the service and the location, so whoever is on duty can act on it without opening the record.

Why it's here

Every one of the marketplace decks on this page argues that the platform layer — matching, routing, records, notification — is where the value sits. This is that layer, made small and made real: routed, stored and notified in four modules. The router is the whole point. Adding a service category means adding a branch, not rewriting the flow.

Scenario blueprint, Make
